SpaceX Lands Their Rocket. In the Dark. From Very High Orbit.

The "edge of space" is not a very high orbit. This booster never made to orbit and there is nothing in the article mentioning it landing from orbit. The velocities involved with orbiting a vehicle versus the velocities involved with a booster on a ballistic trajectory are vastly different. Any energy put into the system has to be pulled out of it on descent. This is (loosely) why they heat up on re-entry...you are pulling that energy out of the system.

The Wired articles headline is factually accurate and infinitely more cool:

SpaceX Landed a Freaking Rocket on a Robot Boat in the Dark

Edit: on re-reading this, I sound a lot more cranky than I intended to. This is a VERY cool feat. I was mildly disappointed that it wasn't from a high orbit. Rocket And orbital mechanics utterly fascinate me, and I was looking forward to digging into how they solved some of the challenges inherent in de-orbiting a booster, having it survive re-entry, and land on a ship.

Well, it was descending at 2km/s (fast enough to make it from Boston to NYC in 3 minutes), whereas the one they launched last month to the ISS was traveling around 1km/s. The second stage for this rocket will reach around 22,000 miles whereas the ISS is sitting in LEO, so yea, from a very high orbit. Maybe I should have said very fast instead.

Around 22,000 miles (35,000k km) puts it into geostationary territory. Orbital velocities for LEO start at around 6.3 km/s, but at 35000 km it would only be about 3km/sec. How high was it when the booster separated from the upper stage?

2 km/s is just south of Mach 6, which is slightly faster than we have managed to get scramjets going in the atmosphere, so yeah, those are respectable numbers to survive.
